overview.title: Student & Teacher Overview: Lesson 28
overview.text: In this signature modeling lesson, you will apply algebra to real-world civic finance: the United States progressive income tax system. You will discover that tax brackets represent a continuous, piecewise linear function where each higher rate applies only to income within that specific marginal bracket.
outcomes: Calculate taxable income from gross income by accounting for standard deductions and exemptions.
Model marginal progressive taxation using piecewise linear functions $T(x)$.
Explain the critical difference between marginal tax rate and effective average tax rate.
overview.teacherInsight: Dispel the pervasive public myth that entering a higher tax bracket reduces net take-home pay. Progressive tax brackets are marginal: only the dollars earned ABOVE the bracket threshold are taxed at the higher percentage!

vocabulary.definition: The tax rate applied to the last dollar of income earned within a specific bracket.
The actual percentage of total income paid in taxes: (Total Tax Paid / Total Income) * 100%.
The amount of gross income used to calculate tax liability, after subtracting allowable exemptions and deductions.

practiceQuestions.question: If single tax brackets are 10% on the first $10,000 and 20% on any amount above $10,000, how much tax is owed on $15,000 of taxable income?
Why does earning more money and moving into a higher tax bracket NEVER result in less take-home pay?
options: Because only the dollars above the bracket threshold are taxed at the higher marginal rate.
Because higher tax brackets have lower percentages.
Because tax brackets only apply to corporate profits.
Because all income below $100,000 is tax-free.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Progressive tax brackets are marginal. Dollars within lower brackets remain taxed at lower rates; only the additional earnings are taxed at the higher rate.
